headlines.article_text: Meta (META) Q3 2026 earnings report: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg demonstrates Muse, Meta's artificial intelligence agent, during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026. Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta is slated to report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and investors will be looking for signs that the company's latest artificial intelligence efforts will bolster future sales. Here's what analysts polled by LSEG are expecting: Earnings per share : $5.75 Revenue : $63.2 billion It's been a big quarter for Mark Zuckerberg's company due to the initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September and shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022. Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday. Wall Street will likely be monitoring for whether Meta plans to increase its data center-related capital expenditures, or capex, to further develop the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models. The company revealed in July during its second-quarter earnings that it narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to come in between $130 billion and $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its prior range. All that spending resulted in Meta's free cash flow in the period shrinking to $784 million from $8.55 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Analysts expect Meta's capex to swell to $196.3 billion in 2027, according to FactSet. Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, is expected to come in at 3.65 billion, according to StreetAccount, almost flat from the prior quarter. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram. 16 Min Ago Meta sets the stage for hyperscaler earnings watch now VIDEO 4:39 04:39 AI capex cycle has 2-3 more years to run, says economist Access Middle East Meta will be the first hyperscaler to reveal quarterly financials during this tech earnings cycle, with Alphabet , Microsoft and Amazon slated to report next week. The four companies combined have called for roughly $730 billion in capital expenditures this year as they stock up on graphics processing units and AI systems and look to build massive data centers around the globe . Analysts polled by FactSet expect that number to hit around $1 trillion next year, led by Alphabet, which is projected to spend over $310 billion. The stepped up spending comes as interest rates soar and concerns intensify that AI revenue won't justify the costs. Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report earnings next Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday. — Jonathan Vanian 29 Min Ago Meta’s legal headaches and state AG settlement watch now VIDEO 12:01 12:01 Watch CNBC's full interview with California AG Rob Bonta Squawk on the Street Meta's past quarter wasn't all AI agents and good vibes. The social media giant agreed in August to pay nearly $17 billion to settle a major lawsuit involving a group of state attorneys general, including California's Rob Bonta. The trial centered around allegations that Meta misled the public about the true scope of child mental health related harms caused by certain design elements of apps like Facebook and Instagram , including recommendation algorithms. Meta's state AG settlement could cause the company to miss on third-quarter earnings per share due to the related $10 billion legal charge that "the street has not yet accounted for," Wolfe Research analysts wrote in a Monday note. The company still faces numerous personal injury claims and a separate federal case involving a group of nationwide school districts that also focus on allegations that apps like Instagram have had detrimental effects on the well being of children. — Jonathan Vanian

headlines.summary: Intel has installed the first major structural truss at its delayed Ohio chip fab, but the company has yet to announce a major outside customer.
headlines.article_text: Intel hits construction milestone at delayed Ohio chip fab Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel’s first Ohio fab was originally expected to begin production in 2025. Operations are now targeted for 2030 or 2031. Intel says construction and tool installation are underway at its next Arizona fab, with operations expected by the end of 2028. Reported discussions with SK Hynix could bring memory production to the Ohio site, but no deal has been confirmed. In this article INTC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the annual Computex trade show in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2026. Tsai Hsin-han | Reuters Intel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix , could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans. When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus. The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans. Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab , producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028. But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices. Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since. Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Apple and Broadcom , "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein. Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there." headlines.article_text: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings report Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla's earnings report comes a day after SpaceX announced better-than-expected profit and revenue. On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the boards of both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. Tesla shares are down 14% so far this year, underperforming all of the company's tech megacap peers. In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Tech billionaire and Tesla founder Elon Musk at a meeting. Johannes Neudecker | Picture Alliance | Getty Images On SpaceX's earnings call late Tuesday, CEO Elon Musk , who also runs Tesla , took a break from talking about financial results to tell investors that it would be a "good idea" to merge his two companies, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. Musk will be back in public after market close on Wednesday, this time to discuss Tesla earnings. Here's what Wall Street is expecting, according to estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 43 cents estimated Revenue: $27.9 billion estimated Should Tesla fail to top expectations, the company would see a slight decrease in revenue from $28.1 billion a year earlier. Tesla has recorded double-digit growth in each of the two prior quarters, but revenue dropped in three of four quarters in 2025, as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit. Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications. While Tesla still counts on auto sales for the bulk of its revenue, Musk sees the company's future in robotaxis and humanoid robots. That's putting the focus on capital expenditures, which are expected to top $25 billion this year, based on a prior forecast, up from about $8.5 billion in 2025. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, Oct. 15, 2026. In this still image taken from a handout video the Roadster comes to a landing using rocket thrusters. Tesla | Via Reuters One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction. "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the SpaceX earnings call, responding to a question about a potential merger. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said. Musk pointed to the company's potential to cooperate on AI software, chip design, Terafab and robotics. Tesla is already using Grok AI technology, developed by SpaceX, to power AI assistants in customer cars, and to help control the company's Optimus humanoid robots now in development. Tesla's stock price is down 14% this year, after rallying on Wednesday, underperforming all of its megacap tech peers. SpaceX went public in June, and is up from its $150 IPO price after its post-earnings pop. Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja told investors on the company's last earnings call in July that automotive margins had been challenged this year by rising interest rates and energy costs. But he also touted growing revenue from Full Self-Driving (Supervised), sometimes referred to as FSD, the partially automated driving system Tesla sells for $99 per month. FSD doesn't make Tesla vehicles safe to use without a human driver, and the company markets the system as Assisted Driving in Europe. Taneja said Tesla reached close to 1.5 million paid FSD customers globally as of the end of June. headlines.article_text: Musk's Trump Account SpaceX stock is 'tip of the iceberg': Gerstner Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points In an X post on Monday, Elon Musk said that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, said on Wednesday that the gift would go to Trump Accounts in an exclusive interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," said Gerstner. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:47 06:47 Brad Gerstner on Trump Accounts: One of the most successful changes to our social contract in 100 years Squawk Box Elon Musk said earlier this week that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year, and CEO of Altimeter Capital Brad Gerstner said Wednesday that the stock donations would come via Trump Accounts . If it happens, that donation of $10.5 billion worth of shares is just the beginning, according to Gerstner, the founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, the new tax-deferred investing accounts for kids. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," Gerstner told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "This is the most giving country on the planet," he said. "I told the president, I think I can raise $100 billion over the course of the next 12 months to sponsor all of the kids in America." In addition to Musk, Gerstner said he had also talked to "every major tech CEO and founder." A $100-billion fundraising target would represent about one-sixth of all U.S. charitable giving. Altogether, Americans donated $592.5 billion in 2024, according to the latest data from the National Philanthropic Trust . Gerstner has also committed about $35 million to help seed the investment accounts for kids in his home state of Indiana. Read more CNBC personal finance coverage CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September, which allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . "The Treasury targeted this carve-out at mega-donors and large philanthropic foundations, such as the Dells, who made a multibillion-dollar charitable pledge," said Adam Bergman, founder of IRA Financial and a tax attorney based in Miami. "It allows them to donate large blocks of publicly traded stock without triggering substantial capital-gains taxes." The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale gifts, and a number of other philanthropists are poised to participate, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano also told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. "They range from small to mega," he said. "We do have mega donors in the nine-digit range, you know, bunches of them." In the broader world of charitable giving, Treasury's temporary regulations also give donors unusual influence over children's investments , according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. Future Trump Account expansion "As @TrumpAccounts continues to grow we look forward to more philanthropists joining the movement and helping children across America jumpstart their financial future," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an X post Monday . The latest Trump Account comments come weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children . Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts , are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $ 1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury. Gerstner also said Wednesday that there is a push to expand access to the accounts to all U.S. citizens under age 40. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today," he said. "So if Elon says then, I want to give to everyone under 40, or OpenAI says I want to give to everyone under 40, there's a vehicle, there's a vessel that they can start compounding in….those are the types of things we are working on." In addition to more than 70 million children under 18 in the U.S., about 90 million U.S. citizens are between 18 and 40 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. However, expanding Trump Accounts to Americans under age 40 would require a legislative change from Congress. In an X post on Tuesday , Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called the proposed expansion a "game-changer," and said he would "lead the bill in the Senate to make it happen." Gerstner told CNBC on Wednesday that expanding the Trump Account age limit is "wildly popular" among Congressional Democrats and Republicans. But it's unclear whether the proposal has the legislative backing needed to become law. headlines.title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge
headlines.summary: Wall Street’s Big Three have generated $52 billion in equity trading revenue this year, capturing about 80% of the market on rising margin lending to hedge funds.
headlines.article_text: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley dominate AI stock boom Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan captured nearly 80% of top five bank equity trading revenues so far this year, generating a combined $52 billion. Growth was driven by "insatiable" hedge fund borrowing for leveraged bets on AI hardware and Asian semiconductor supply chains. The Big Three’s massive balance sheets allow them to absorb possible losses and handle risks that force smaller rivals to cede share. Relaxed rules around leverage helped to unlock bank balance sheets to meet record demand, though bodies including the International Monetary Fund cautioned against rising leverage. In this article GS JPM MS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT David Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs (L), Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan (C), and Ted Pick, CEO of Morgan Stanley. CNBC | Getty Images | CNBC Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go. The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul. But it's Wall Street's Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry's most lucrative arena: Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley have made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total. "When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that's pretty much it," Mike Mayo , Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. "They've been best positioned to take advantage of this market." Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, exchange-traded funds and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets. Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three's prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products. Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week. At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activities jumped 96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don't break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic. "I like your 'insatiable demand for capital' point. That feels about right," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the bank's third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands. "In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms," Barnum said. That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say. The performance gap between Wall Street's giants and rivals including Bank of America and Citigroup highlights a widening divide in capital markets. "For clients, the value isn't just a price on one trade, it's coverage and continuity," Rachid Alaoui, JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. "You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility." Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can't underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share. U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from the retreat of European banks including Credit Suisse from the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan . "Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses," Chan said. "If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties." Picks and shovels While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia. Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the "picks and shovels" of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said. For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine. However, trading executives point out that transaction taxes and stamp duties are included in top-line revenue, artificially inflating Asia prime totals. There is also no agreed-upon definition of what equities trading revenue should include, so some banks include business lines like clearing services that others exclude from their stock trading totals, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult. But that doesn't change the overall momentum of the business, boosted by a stock rally that began in October 2022, weeks before OpenAI released ChatGPT. "We're still in a stock-based world," Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick said on the firm's earnings call. "Equities are still, all things being equal, the attractive asset class." VIDEO 9:35 09:35 Watch CNBC's full interview with Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick While the CEOs of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have said the AI build-out is still in its early years, if AI turns out to be not as transformative as hoped, a downturn could impact those banks more than others, analysts said. The boom has also drawn some concern over the possible risks posed by hedge funds. The International Monetary Fund warned this month that growing leverage , crowded positions and correlated selling from hedge funds could create potential stability risks. The IMF estimated that global hedge fund assets had reached $13 trillion. In August, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said industrywide leverage was "the highest it's ever been ," though he stopped short of calling the risk big enough to pose a threat to the financial markets. Wall Street executives and analysts pointed out that the industry wasn't fazed by the meltdown of several hedge funds this summer. While the hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness , garnered the most headlines, several smaller firms also experienced a forced unwinding. Prime brokers have learned to leap on margin calls and quickly take down risk when markets move against clients, JPMorgan's Alaoui said. "In the summer, some investors had positions they were forced to unwind," he told CNBC. "They deleveraged, risk came down, and the market moved on." 'Known unknowns' Another factor driving the equities boom: Trump administration regulators have eased some leverage rules for the largest U.S. banks, giving them more room to expand balance sheet-heavy businesses including prime brokerage.
